meaning.evidence: Every instruction survives: the radiator and muslin, "The system holds about three gallons", the ten-gallon tank, the two pet cocks, the lever notches. Additions hang off the original's warnings: "and you'll blow your arse to kingdom come", "give you a hell of a whack".

sense.evidence: Terms fit: "under its own steam", "beats hard water hands down", "the more grunt you get" for power, "it pays to check", "once you've had a bit of a go" for a little experience.

authenticity.evidence: Sounds like an Aussie mechanic talking you through it: "make bloody sure there's no naked flames", "keep it properly topped up", "the bits that need it". Spellings localised: "petrol", "carburettor", "vapour".

register.evidence: Casual and clearly Aussie throughout, but closer to a level 4 than a full pub yarn; long stretches are plain: "The throttle should usually be opened about five or six notches." Swearing within uncle-bob.

tone.evidence: Keeps the manual's practical care, though the added "you'll blow your arse to kingdom come" pushes the safety warning toward a joke.

flow.evidence: Reads smoothly: "Keep pouring water in till you're dead sure the radiator and the cylinder water jackets are both full."

variety.evidence: Varied, though "'cause" recurs: "'cause hard water can have alkalies", "'cause the fumes are extremely volatile", "'cause the air for several feet around".

essence.evidence: Unmistakably the 1919 Q&A manual, headings and cross-references kept: "(See Cut No. 18, also chapter on Lubrication.)"

problems.why: Colour on the warning, but it tips a sober safety note toward a gag.

A.summary: A natural, faithful mechanic's-voice retelling, a shade lighter than level 5.

meaning.evidence: All content kept, almost verbatim: "Upon receipt of the car see that a supply of medium light, high-grade gas engine oil is poured into the crank case".

sense.evidence: The few swaps fit ("bunged up", "petrol"), but "a brand-spankin'-new car" and "a beaut plan" strain in a manual's advice line.

authenticity.evidence: The original's formal prose with dropped g's and a few words bolted on: "the vapour is flamin' volatile'n travels rapidly", "it's a beaut plan to examine the radiator frequently". US forms left: "What about Gasoline?", "carburetor".

register.evidence: Largely untranslated, far lighter than level 5: "The water supply should be replenished as often as may be found necessary."

tone.evidence: The manual's plain instructional tone survives because little is changed: "Care should be taken not to advance the spark lever too far".

flow.evidence: Clunky joins where dialect meets formal prose: "flamin' volatile'n travels rapidly", "If perfectly clean water can't be obtained it's advisable".

variety.evidence: Leans on g-dropping and "outta" ("run outta the overflow pipe", "runs outta the upper cock"); little slang otherwise.

essence.evidence: Recognisably the original, since it mostly is the original: "(See chapter on Cooling System.)"

B.summary: The original with g-dropping and a few words swapped in; far lighter than the brief.

meaning.evidence: Every instruction survives: the muslin, three gallons, the ten-gallon tank, the two pet cocks, the notches, the back kick. Nothing invented.

sense.evidence: Mostly fits: "lay yer mitts on", "bunged up", "come hell or high water", "the more grunt ya get". "Before ya give the car a burl" strains: a burl is a try or a spin, so it reads as before you take it for a drive, close but not starting.

authenticity.evidence: Mostly natural ("flamin' volatile", "top-shelf", "start her proper"), but the dialect spelling is dense: "muck gets in 'n blocks up", "alkalies 'n other salts", "ya find ya need to".

register.evidence: A full, broad voice right through, as level 5 asks: "If ya can't lay yer mitts on perfectly clean water", "don't ever, come hell or high water, let it get below the lower cock". One "bloody", within the brief.

tone.evidence: Keeps the careful instructional tone under the voice; warnings stay warnings: "Watch ya don't advance the spark lever too far".

flow.evidence: Readable, though the " 'n " and "ya" contractions clutter: "the faster the engine runs 'n the more grunt ya get".

variety.evidence: Good range of idiom, but "cos" recurs four times and "ya" constantly.

essence.evidence: Unmistakably the Ford manual, Q&A headings and references kept: "(See Cut No. 18, also chapter on Lubrication.)"
